neuralnets.q: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
options: A weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation
The average of its inputs, rounded to 0 or 1
A lookup of the input in a table of stored examples
The distance between the input and the nearest training point
neuralnets.why: A neuron multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias and applies an activation such as ReLU or sigmoid.

options: The final prediction for a new input
The gradient of the loss for every weight, using the chain rule
The best learning rate for the optimizer
Which training examples are mislabelled
neuralnets.why: Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss back through each layer to get every weight's gradient. The forward pass makes predictions.

neuralnets.q: A customer's model shows falling training loss but rising validation loss after epoch 12. What do you suggest first?
options: Train for more epochs until validation loss comes back down
Increase the learning rate so it escapes the problem
Keep the epoch 12 checkpoint and add early stopping and regularisation
Add more hidden layers so it can learn the validation data too
neuralnets.why: This is overfitting. Early stopping keeps the best checkpoint, and dropout or weight decay reduce memorising. More epochs or a bigger network make it worse.

neuralnets.q: A team's loss jumps up and down wildly and sometimes becomes NaN. What is the most likely first thing to check?
options: The number of output classes
Whether the test set is too small
Whether dropout is set too low
Whether the learning rate is too high
neuralnets.why: Too large a step overshoots the minimum and can make values explode. Lowering the learning rate or scaling inputs is the usual first fix.

neuralnets.q: Spot the mistake: 'We removed the activation functions to speed up our 5-layer network. It should learn the same patterns.'
options: Without activations the layers collapse into one linear function and cannot learn curved patterns
Removing activations only affects speed, so the claim is correct
Activations are only needed in the output layer, so it is fine
It will learn the same patterns but needs more epochs
neuralnets.why: A chain of linear layers is still linear, so the network can only draw straight boundaries. The nonlinear bend is what makes depth useful.

dlarch.q: Why do CNNs suit images better than plain dense networks?
options: They read pixels one at a time in order
They reuse small filters across the image, so fewer weights detect a pattern anywhere
They do not need any training data
They convert images into text first
dlarch.why: Convolution slides the same small filter everywhere (weight sharing), so an edge detector works in any position with few weights.

dlarch.q: What was the main problem plain RNNs had with long sequences?
options: They could not process numbers, only words
They needed attention to run at all
The training signal faded or exploded as it passed back through many steps
They required images as input
dlarch.why: Backpropagating through many time steps multiplies the gradient repeatedly, so it vanishes or explodes. LSTMs eased this with gates.

dlarch.q: A customer has 2,000 labelled photos and wants an image classifier. What is the sensible starting point?
options: Fine-tune a pretrained image model, starting with a new head
Train a new CNN from scratch on the 2,000 photos
Label 100,000 more photos before building anything
Use an RNN so the photos are read in order
dlarch.why: Transfer learning reuses features learned from huge datasets and works well with a few thousand labels. From scratch usually underperforms at this size.

dlarch.q: A customer asks why their 7 billion parameter model will not load on an 8 GB GPU. What is the best explanation?
options: The GPU needs a driver update to handle large models
In 16-bit the weights alone need about 14 GB, more than the card's memory
GPUs cannot run language models, only images
The model needs to be converted into a CNN first
dlarch.why: Each 16-bit weight takes 2 bytes, so 7 billion weights need about 14 GB. Quantisation or a bigger card or hosted API are the options.

dlarch.q: Spot the mistake: 'Transformers are the best model, so we will use one for our 20-column sales table.'
options: Transformers can only be used for images
Tables must always use an LSTM
The table needs to be at least 100 columns first
For small tabular data, gradient boosted trees usually beat deep learning
dlarch.why: Architecture should follow the data shape. On typical business tables, boosted trees are usually more accurate, faster and easier to explain.

rlhf.q: In reinforcement learning, what is a policy?
options: The reward the environment gives
The data used to pretrain the model
The agent's rule for choosing an action in each situation
The penalty for drifting from a reference model
rlhf.why: The policy maps states to actions. RL training changes the policy so it earns more total reward.

rlhf.q: In a multi-armed bandit, what does epsilon control in epsilon-greedy?
options: How often the agent picks a random arm to explore
How much each arm pays out
How many arms there are
How fast rewards are paid
rlhf.why: With probability epsilon it explores a random arm; otherwise it exploits the best arm so far. Epsilon 0 can lock onto a poor arm.

rlhf.q: A customer says 'retrain the hosted model with RLHF so it stops agreeing with angry users'. What do you do first?
options: Start collecting 100,000 human comparisons
Explain it is a learned tendency, then try prompt rules, evidence and an eval set
Switch to a model with no alignment training
Increase the temperature so answers vary more
rlhf.why: Hosted models are aligned by the provider. Prompting, tools and evals are the cheap first levers; fine-tuning comes later if supported and justified.

rlhf.q: A team has chosen and rejected answer pairs and wants the simplest way to train an open model on them. What fits best?
options: Build a reward model, then run PPO with a KL penalty
Train only on the rejected answers
Pretrain a new model from scratch
Run DPO directly on the pairs
rlhf.why: DPO trains on preference pairs without a separate reward model or RL loop, so it runs like ordinary fine-tuning.

rlhf.q: Spot the mistake: 'We removed the KL penalty so the model can maximise the reward model score freely.'
options: The model may exploit the reward model's quirks, known as reward hacking
The KL penalty only affects speed, so nothing changes
Without it the reward model stops training
The KL penalty is only used in bandits
rlhf.why: The KL penalty keeps the model close to the SFT version. Without it the policy finds answers that score highly but are not actually better.
